data.title: Bitcoin ETF inflows hit $3 billion in eight days as institutions return
data.description:
US spot Bitcoin ETFs took in approximately $3 billion in net inflows between September 17 and September 25, 2026. That stretch ranks among the strongest buying periods since the funds launched in January 2024.

The burst did something months of grinding could not. It pushed the year's flow tally out of the red.

Hedge funds, often cast as the fast money behind ETF surges, appear to have played only a minor role this time. The buying looks more like a broad institutional return than a trading desk making a short-term bet.

The peak week alone delivered $2.4 billion in net inflows. That was the largest weekly haul since October 2025.

BlackRock's IBIT led the pack with around $1.2 billion during that peak week. Fidelity's FBTC added roughly $702 million, while ARK 21Shares' ARKB brought in about $295 million.

The biggest single day came on September 21, 2026, when inflows hit nearly $999 million.

The rebound matters most against where flows stood earlier in the year. By mid-July, the funds were sitting on a year-to-date deficit of about $5.8 billion.

By late September, that hole had become a modest net positive of about $934 million.

The flows lined up with Bitcoin's price recovery. During the period, Bitcoin traded between $82,000 and $87,000.

Zoom out and the third quarter looks even stronger. Q3 2026 recorded $6.34 billion in Bitcoin ETF inflows, the highest of any quarter this year.

Cumulative net inflows since launch reached approximately $57-58 billion by early October 2026. Total assets under management sat around $105-110 billion over the same window.

The party did not last. Net outflows resumed in early October 2026, including a $244 million outflow on October 8.

When the spot ETFs debuted in January 2024, they offered something new. Traditional investors could get Bitcoin exposure through a brokerage account, no crypto exchange or private keys required.

Who is buying shapes how durable a rally might be. Hedge fund flows often tie to basis trades, where funds buy ETF shares and short futures to capture a price gap. That kind of buying can unwind quickly once the spread closes.

Broader institutional demand tends to be stickier. If allocators are adding Bitcoin as a portfolio slice rather than a trade, the money is less likely to sprint for the exit at the first wobble.

The late-September data leans toward the second scenario.

For investors, the clearest signal is a shift in sentiment. Wiping out a deficit of about $5.8 billion suggests institutions still see Bitcoin as a legitimate portfolio holding, not just a speculative side bet.

The concentration in BlackRock's IBIT also stands out. With around $1.2 billion of the peak-week inflows, the largest issuer kept widening its lead over Fidelity and ARK 21Shares.

Still, the October outflows serve as a reminder against reading too much into any single week. A $244 million exit on October 8 shows that sentiment can flip as fast as it arrived.

Bitcoin's price range also deserves attention. Inflows clustered while Bitcoin recovered into the $82,000 to $87,000 band.

What to watch next is whether early October outflows prove to be a pause or a turn. If the year-to-date total of about $934 million slips back toward negative territory, the September surge will look more like a relief rally than a trend.

If inflows resume and cumulative totals push past the approximately $57-58 billion mark, the case for steady institutional adoption gets stronger.

data.title: SEBI turns bond ratings into a consumer-friendly traffic-light system
data.description:
In a move to make bond investing easier for retail investors, market regulator SEBI has introduced a mandatory Credit Risk-o-Meter for debt securities. Issuers and Online Bond Platform Providers (OBPPs) must display the colour-coded risk meter in offer documents, abridged prospectuses, private-placement memorandums, advertisements, and the web and mobile platforms of OBPPs.

The framework covers listed and proposed-to-be-listed non-convertible securities, commercial papers, securitised debt instruments, security receipts and structured debt or market-linked debentures, whether issued through public issues or private placements. The provisions will come into force 45 days after the October 7, 2026, circular.

The pictorial representation is not new to the industry. This colour-coded Risk-o-Meter is used in mutual fund disclosures. SEBI introduced product labelling for mutual funds more than a decade ago and subsequently developed the current Risk-o-Meter framework. All mutual fund schemes must display a six-level Risk-o-Meter, ranging from Low to Very High risk, which is recalibrated monthly based on the underlying portfolio. The new bond Credit Risk-o-Meter adopts a similar colour-coded approach, moving from green for the lowest credit risk to red for the highest risk of default.

What is it?

While a mutual fund Risk-o-Meter captures multiple risks, including market, interest-rate, liquidity and credit risks, the new Credit Risk-o-Meter focuses exclusively on the credit risk associated with a debt security. It is intended to help small investors understand the risk of an issuer failing to meet its financial obligations.

Traditionally, investors have relied on credit ratings assigned by credit rating agencies (CRAs) such as Crisil, ICRA, CARE Ratings and India Ratings. While institutional investors and experienced market participants are familiar with rating symbols such as AAA, AA and BBB, retail investors may find these labels difficult to interpret. By translating rating symbols into familiar colour-coded risk categories, SEBI aims to make credit risk easier to assess.

Under the framework, credit ratings will be mapped to six risk categories. The first, Lowest Credit Risk, covers AAA-rated long-term debt securities and A1+-rated short-term instruments.

The second, Very Low Credit Risk, covers AA-rated securities, including the AA+ and AA- variants, and A1-rated short-term instruments.

The third, Low Credit Risk, includes A-rated securities and A2-rated short-term instruments.

BBB-rated securities fall under Moderate Credit Risk, alongside A3-rated short-term instruments. BB-rated securities are placed in the Moderate Risk of Default category, alongside A4+-rated short-term instruments.

The final category, High to Very High Risk of Default, covers B-, C- and D-rated securities, including their applicable rating modifiers, as well as A4- and D-rated short-term instruments. The colour spectrum progresses from green through yellow, brown and orange to red. The traffic-light format is designed to make differences in credit risk more immediately visible.

Where a CRA identifies an issuer as “Issuer Not Cooperating” (INC), the Credit Risk-o-Meter must indicate the INC status, with an arrow pointing towards it.

Issuers and OBPPs must additionally disclose the CRA’s name and the actual credit rating of the debt security in text below the meter. For unsecured debt instruments, the word “unsecured” must appear in bold red text. Where a security has ratings from multiple CRAs, the meter must reflect the lowest rating, although all ratings may be disclosed alongside it.

On mobile interfaces, the meter may be condensed, provided the entire risk spectrum remains visible and an arrow points to the product’s specific risk level. Selecting the information (‘i’) icon must bring up the detailed version, consistent with the web display.

What does it mean for investors?

Retail participation in bonds has grown alongside the emergence of online bond platforms, which allow investors to access corporate debt more conveniently. However, easier access does not necessarily mean investors fully understand the risks involved. A colour-coded meter could help bridge this gap by making the credit quality of a debt security easier to interpret at a glance.

SEBI has clarified that the meter reflects only credit risk and does not constitute investment advice or a recommendation to invest. It does not capture all the other risks associated with debt securities, including market and liquidity risks.

The distinction is particularly important for unsecured perpetual bonds, such as additional tier-1 (AT1) bonds issued by banks. SEBI has prescribed an additional disclaimer for these instruments, warning that the meter does not reflect their unique structural risks and that investors could lose their entire invested capital.

In essence, SEBI’s initiative seeks to make credit risk more visible. Investors can use the meter as a quick screening tool to understand where a security stands on the credit-risk spectrum. A green indicator signals a lower assessed credit risk, while orange and red indicate elevated risk. However, a lower credit-risk category does not automatically make a bond suitable for every investor. Yield, maturity, liquidity, issuer fundamentals, instrument structure and portfolio allocation must also be considered before investing.

data.title: Rising rates: What should your debt strategy be?
data.description:
In last week’s Big Story, we talked about why rising bond yields (and central banks hiking rates) globally, could represent a regime change for equity investors. As global interest rates climb after a prolonged phase of repression, investors may need to lower their return expectations from equities, at least at the market level. But there’s a positive side to this yield spike too — it opens up better return opportunities for debt investors.

In India, interest rates never went to zero. Therefore, the rise in yields poses less of a shock than in say, the US or Japan. However, with the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) restarting a rate hike cycle after a four-year gap, Indian debt investors may need to recalibrate their strategies to benefit from higher rates. To know what kind of bonds to own now, you need to gauge the direction of interest rates and the quantum of the change.

How market rates behaved

Today, whether you consider long-term interest rates or short-term, the direction is clearly up.

Long-term bond yields in India are pegged to the 10-year government security, which acts as the floor for long-term borrowing costs. After the Iran war broke out in February 2026 and oil prices surged, Indian bond markets worried about rising subsidies forcing the Central government to overshoot its deficit target. Therefore, the yield on longer-tenure Central government securities spiked first. Between January and April 2026, the yield on the 10-year G-Sec (government bond) rose from 6.6 per cent to 6.9 per cent. During this period, inflation remained low and there was no talk of policy rate hikes; so short-term interest rates stayed put.

With State governments on a borrowing binge, yields on SDLs (State government loans) spiked more, from 7.5 per cent to 7.9 per cent. Corporate bonds, which usually trade at a spread over G-Secs saw their yields increase. They rose from 7 per cent to 7.5 per cent for one-year AAA-rated bonds and 7.25 per cent to 7.6 per cent for three-year AAA-rated bonds. However, a frugal budget, which stayed with a 4.3 per cent fiscal deficit target in March and fuel price hikes in May, thereafter allayed fears about the deficit overshooting. Therefore, between April and October 2026, India’s 10-year government bond yields have risen only marginally from 6.9 per cent to 7.25 per cent.

However, yields on short-term bonds have played catch-up in this period. In recent months, it has become quite clear that a quick resolution to the Iran war is unlikely. Elevated energy prices and the long-lasting El Nino, have thus put upward pressure on domestic inflation, propping up CPI (consumer price index) inflation from 3.4 per cent in March to 4.8 per cent by August. This prompted bond markets to begin pricing in rate hikes by the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), with yields on 91-day to 364-day treasury bills rising from 5.3-5.6 per cent in April to 5.5-6.2 per cent now.

This week, the MPC met the market’s expectations by raising the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5 per cent. It also indicated that further rate hikes were in the offing, by talking of “calibrated tightening”.

What’s priced in

The above analysis shows that the direction of rates is pretty clear today. But how much will rates rise from here and how much of this is already priced into market yields? This is an important question because bond markets, like stock markets, price in events much before they happen.

On the first question, it is too early for a definitive answer. In the post-Covid rate hiking cycle that lasted from 2022 to 2023, the MPC hiked rates from 4 per cent to 6.5 per cent (250 basis points). In the extended cycle from 2010 to 2014, it hiked rates from 5 per cent all the way to 8 per cent, a 300-basis point hike. However, there have been shallower cycles too like 2017-18 when rates went up just 50 basis points from 6 per cent to 6.5 per cent. The quantum of hikes this time around will depend on incoming data on inflation, growth and capital flows. But it would be good to brace for an extended cycle.

On the second question of what the market is pricing in, the bond market seems to be pricing in another 70-75 basis points in rate hikes. One, the 364-day Treasury bill trades at about 6.28 per cent now, which is 78 basis points above the repo rate; T-bills yields have usually traded pretty close to the repo rate. Two, the 10-year G-Sec yield, at 7.23 per cent, is now 173 basis points above the repo rate. The average spread between the 10-year G-Sec and the repo has historically hovered at 80-100 basis points. This suggests that the additional 73 basis points is the market expectation for further rate increases.

Your debt strategy

This means three things for your debt strategy:

* With rate hikes just beginning, it may be risky to lock into bonds or debt mutual funds with long tenures (five years plus). Should market yields continue to shoot up or rate hikes go on for long, you can lose money by buying into long-duration bonds or debt funds today. In the past 15 years or so, 10-year G-Sec yields in India have topped out close to 8 per cent. Therefore, it would be good to wait for levels of 7.5-8 per cent on the 10-year G-Sec before considering long-duration bonds or debt funds. If you have surpluses to deploy now, it is safer today to invest them in bonds or debt funds with tenures of upto three years. This way, you can benefit from further rate hikes for as long as this cycle continues.

* Among three-year instruments, high-quality corporate bonds look attractive at yields of over 8 per cent. One- year and three-year AAA corporate bonds now trade at spreads of 142 and 125 basis points respectively over similar maturity G-Secs, which is high from a historical perspective. This makes such bonds a good buy. Currently, bonds from M&M Financial, Tata Capital, rated AAA and maturing in 2029, offer yields of about 8.1 per cent. PSU bonds from IRFC, HUDCO and SIDBI, maturing in 2029, offer about 7.65-7.8 per cent.

* While yields on G-Secs and corporate bonds are already factoring in the rise in policy rates, the fixed deposit market is yet to catch up. Large banks like SBI and ICICI still offer just 6.3-6.5 per cent for three-year deposits. Small finance banks, which traditionally offer the best FD deals, offer only 7.5-8 per cent, that too for special windows. Highly-rated NBFCs like Sundaram Finance and Bajaj Finance offer 7.25-7.75 per cent on three-year deposits. This could be due to banks enjoying comfortable liquidity after their FCNR (B) flows.

Debt investors fishing for higher returns today should thus stick to corporate bonds or debt mutual funds, opting for the shortest tenure possible within three years.

The author is a Contributing Editor

data.title: Fidelity’s Global Macro Director Jurrien Timmer Says Bitcoin Has Bottomed And Should Beat Gold Here On
data.description:
Key points:
  • Timmer said Bitcoin tested $60,000 before falling to $58,000, suggesting a bottom. He added that Bitcoin winters last 9 to 12 months.
  • He expects Bitcoin and gold to rise and said gold's fair value is $5,000, but speculators drove it to $5,600.
  • He said rising 10-year Treasury yields, around 5.3%, were pressuring stocks and causing a stealth correction. 

Bitcoin (BTC) has bottomed and should outperform gold from here, according to Fidelity Investments’ Jurrien Timmer. Timmer stated that Bitcoin ended a mild bear market, and its rise above $80,000 confirmed a double bottom, indicating that the price may have found support.

Timmer, the firm’s director of global macro, made the call during an appearance on The Compound & Friends podcast on Friday. Timmer said “60K is a level that I’m going to buy and it went to 58,” and that is a chart pattern in which a price tests a low twice and holds. He said the price looked right earlier this year, but the timing did not. Bitcoin’s winters have tended to last 9 to 12 months, he said. Traders often read it as a sign that a downtrend is over.

He expects both Bitcoin and gold to rally. He said there’s more room for Bitcoin to run. "Bitcoin is going to go up more," he said.

Cycle Model Missed Peak

His cycle model had pointed to a peak close to $150,000 last year, said Timmer. He said Bitcoin topped out at about $126,000. The model plots time and price on logarithmic scales, compressing large moves to make it easier to compare patterns. Each winter is shorter than the previous one, he said. “It’s a maturing asset, right? So, it’s going to moon less and it’s going to swoon less,” he said.

Timmer Says Gold Near $5,000: Warns Rising Treasury Yields Could Trigger Stock Correction

After Bitcoin’s peak, speculators moved out of Bitcoin into gold, Timmer said. That took gold to around $5,600, he said. His model of the global money supply indicates gold should not have risen above $4,800, he said. Fair value is about $5,000 and climbing, he added. Bitcoin priced in gold shows a double bottom too, he said.

Timmer’s take comes with a warning on bonds. The 10-year Treasury yield is around 5.3%, he said. He said rising yields are putting pressure on stocks and creating what he called a stealth correction.

He cited gold, Bitcoin and commodities as ways to diversify a portfolio when stocks and bonds fall together. Could those assets start trading in lockstep with stocks, the hosts asked. Some of them are in danger, he said.

Bitcoin’s price was trading around $82,935, flat over the past 24 hours. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around BTC remained in the ‘bearish’ zone, accompanied by ‘low’ levels over the past day.
